readings.head: {{RunningHeader|unmutable|6631|unobedient}}
readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unmutable†''' (un-mū′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Immutable.

'''unmutilated''' (un-mū′ti-lā-ted), ''a.'' Not mutilated; not deprived of a member or part; entire.

'''unmuzzle''' (un-muz′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''muzzle.''] To loose from a muzzle; remove a muzzle from; hence, figuratively, to free from restraint.
{{smaller block|Ay, marry, now ''unmuzzle'' your wisdom.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2. 74.}}}}

'''unmystery''' (un-mis′tẹ-ri), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''mystery''<sup>1</sup>.] To divest of mystery; make clear or plain. ''Fuller'', Worthies, Hereford, i. 453. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''unnail''' (un-nāl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nail.''] To remove or take out the nails from; unfasten or loosen by removing nails.
{{smaller block|Whiles Joseph of Arimathæa and Nicodemus ''unnail'' our Lord.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Perfection of Painting.}}}}

'''unnamable''' (un-nā′ma̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being named; indescribable. Also ''unnameable.''
{{smaller block|A cloud of ''unnameable'' feeling.
{{right|''Poe'', Imp of the Perverse.}}}}

'''unnamed''' (un-nāmd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not named; not having received a name; hence, not known by name; anonymous.
{{smaller block|''Unnamed'' accusers in the dark.
{{right|''Byron'', Siege of Corinth, iv.}}}}
'''2.''' Not named; not mentioned.
{{smaller block|Be glad thou art ''unnamed.''
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', False One, ii. 1.}}}}

'''unnapkined''' (un-nap′kind), ''a.'' Having no napkin or handkerchief. [Rare.]
readings.c1s2:
{{smaller block|<poem>No pandar’s wither’d paw,
Nor an ''unnapkin’d'' lawyer’s greasy fist,
Hath once slubber’d thee.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, i. 3.}}}}

'''unnapped''' (un-napt′), ''a.'' Not having a nap; made without a nap, as cloth; deprived of nap.

'''unnative''' (un-nā′tiv), ''a.'' Not native; foreign; not natural; not naturalized, as a word.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whence . . . this ''unnative'' fear,
To generous Britons never known before?</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Britannia.}}}}

'''unnatural''' (un-nat̮′ū-ral), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not natural; contrary to nature; monstrous; especially, contrary to the natural feelings: as, ''unnatural'' offenses.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unnatural'' deeds
Do breed ''unnatural'' troubles.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 1. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is well known that the mystery which overhangs what is distant, either in space or time, frequently prevents us from censuring as ''unnatural'' what we perceive to be impossible. {{right|''Macaulay'', History.}}}}
'''2.''' Acting without the affections of our common nature; not having the feelings natural to humanity; being without natural instincts: as, an ''unnatural'' parent.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rome, whose gratitude
Tow’rds her deserved children is enroll’d
In Jove’s own book, like an ''unnatural'' dam,
Should now eat up her own. ''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 293.</poem>}}
'''3.''' Not in conformity to nature; not agreeable to the real character of persons or things; not representing nature; forced; strained; affected; artificial: as, ''unnatural'' images or descriptions.
{{smaller block|All violences and extravagances of a religious fancy are}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unnaturally''' (un-nat̮′ṳ̄-ra̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unnatural manner; in opposition to natural feelings and sentiments. ''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1. 193.

'''unnaturalness''' (un-nat̮′ṳ̄-ral-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unnatural; contrariety to nature.

'''unnature<sup>1</sup>''' (un-nā′t̮ṳ̄r), ''n.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''nature.''] The absence of nature or of the order of nature; the contrary of nature; that which is unnatural.
{{smaller block|So as to be rather ''unnature'', after all, than nature.
{{right|''H. Bushnell.''}}}}

'''unnature<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-nā′t̮ṳ̄r), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nature.''] To change or take away the nature of; endow with a different nature. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.

'''unnavigability''' (un-nav″i-ga̤-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unnavigable. ''Littell’s Living Age'', CLXI. 88.

'''unnavigable''' (un-nav′i-ga̤-bl), ''a.'' Not navigable; incapable of being navigated; that may not be sailed on.
{{smaller block|That ''unnavigable'' stream. ''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal, x. 12.}}

'''unnavigated''' (un-nav′i-gā-ted), ''a.'' Not navigated; not passed over in ships or other vessels; not sailed on or over. ''Cook'', Third Voyage.

'''unnear†''' (un-nēr′), ''prep.'' Not near; not close to; at a distance from.
{{smaller block|Now Cities stand ''vnneere'' the Ocean’s brim.
{{right|''Davies'', Muse’s Sacrifice, p. 51. (''Davies.'')}}}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unnecessarily''' (un-nes′e-sạ̄-ri-li), ''adv.'' In an unnecessary manner; without necessity; needlessly; superfluously. ''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 264.
'''unnecessariness''' (un-nes′e-sạ̄-ri-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unnecessary; needlessness. ''Dr. H. More.''
'''unnecessary''' (un-nes′e-sạ̄-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''unnecessarie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''necessary''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Not necessary; needless; not required by the circumstances of the case; useless: as, ''unnecessary'' labor or care; ''unnecessary'' rigor.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unnecessarie''
Is him to plaunte yf he be wel ysowe.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 143.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''unnecessaries'' (-riz). That which is unnecessary or dispensable.
{{smaller block|<poem>It contains nothing
But rubbish from the other rooms, and ''unnecessaries.''</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, ii. 6.}}}}
'''unnecessity†''' (un-nē-ses′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The contrary of necessity; something unnecessary. ''Sir T. Browne.''
'''unneedful''' (un-nēd′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not needful; not wanted; needless; unnecessary.
{{smaller block|Speake not everye truth, for that is ''vnneedfull.''
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 360.}}}}
'''unneedfully''' (un-nēd′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' Needlessly; unnecessarily. ''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.
'''unneighbored, unneighboured''' (un-nā′bo̤rd), ''a.'' Having no neighbors.
{{smaller block|Scheria, . . . an ''unneighbour’d'' isle,}}
readings.c2s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>And far from all resort of busy man.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, vi.}}}}

¶
'''unneighborliness, unneighbourliness''' (un-nā′-bo̤r-li-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unneighborly. ''The Atlantic'', LXV. 380.

'''unneighborly, unneighbourly''' (un-nā′bo̤r-li), ''a.'' Not neighborly; not in accordance with the duties or obligations of a neighbor; distant; reserved; hence, unkind: as, an ''unneighborly'' act.
{{smaller block|On the West it is separated and secure from ''vnneighbourly'' neighbours by a sandie wildernesse.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 435.}}}}

'''unneighborly†, unneighbourly†''' (un-nā′bo̤r-li), ''adv.'' In an unneighborly manner; distantly; with reserve; hence, unkindly.
{{smaller block|The French . . . have dealt . . . very unfriendly and ''unneighbourly'' to us.
{{right|''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., Edw. VI., an. 1549.}}}}

'''unnervate†''' (un-nėr′vāt), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''nervate'', < ''nerve'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup> (cf. ''enervate'').] Not strong; feeble; enervated. ''W. Broome.''

'''unnerve''' (un-nėrv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nerve''.] To deprive of nerve, force, or strength; weaken; enfeeble; hence, to deprive of power or authority, as a government.
{{smaller block|<poem>With the whiff and wind of his fell sword
The ''unnerved'' father falls. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2. 496.</poem>
Such situations bewilder and ''unnerve'' the weak, but call forth all the strength of the strong.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vii.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|But that beloved name ''unnerved'' my arm.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Sohrab and Rustum.}}}}

¶
'''unnest''' (un-nest′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''unnesten''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nest''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To turn out of a nest; dislodge.
{{smaller block|The eye ''unnested'' from the head cannot see.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 258.}}
The earth on its softly-spinning axle never jars enough to ''unnest'' a bird or wake a child.
{{right|''H. W. Warren'', Recreations in Astronomy, p. 58.}}}}

'''II.'''† ''intrans.'' To leave or depart from a nest or abiding-place (?).
{{smaller block|<poem>O soule! lurking in this wo ''unneste'',
Fle forth out of myn herte and let it breste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 305.}}}}

'''unnestle†''' (un-nes′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nestle''. Cf. ''unnest''.] To deprive of or eject from a nest; dislodge; eject.
{{smaller block|Lucifer . . . will go about to ''unnestle'' and drive out of heaven all the gods.
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 2. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''unneth†''', ''adv.'' Same as ''uneath''.

'''unnetted''' (un-net′ed), ''a.'' Not inclosed in a net or network; unprotected by nets. ''Tennyson'', The Blackbird.

'''unniggard''' (un-nig′ärd), ''a.'' Not niggard or miserly; liberal. ''Sylvester''.

'''unniggardly''' (un-nig′ärd-li), ''a.'' Not niggardly or miserly; unniggard; generous. ''Tucker''.

'''unnimbed''' (un-nimd′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''nimb'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Not having a nimbus; represented as without a nimbus. ''Smith'', Dict. of Christ. Antiq., II. 1400.

'''unnoble'''<sup>1</sup> (un-nō′bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''noble''.] Not
readings.c3s2:
noble; ignoble; mean. {{smaller block|Can there be any nature so ''unnoble'',
Or anger so inhuman, to pursue this? {{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, ii. 1.}}}} ¶ '''unnoble2''' (un-nō′bl), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''noble.''] To deprive of nobility. ''Heywood'', If you Know not me (Works, 1874, I. 236). '''unnobleness''' (un-nō′bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unnoble; meanness. {{smaller block|Whose ''unnobleness'',
Indeed forgetfulness of good — {{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, i. 3.}}}} '''unnobly''' (un-nō′bli), ''adv.'' Not nobly; ignobly. {{smaller block|Why do you deal thus with him? ’tis ''unnobly''. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wit without Money, iv. 1.}}}} '''unnooked''' (un-nu̇kt′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''1 + ''nook'' + ''-ed''2.] Without nooks or crannies; hence, figuratively, without guile; open; simple. {{smaller block|With innocent upreared armes to Heaven,
With my ''unnookt'' simplicitie. {{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iv. 3.}}}} '''unnoted''' (un-nō′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not noted; not observed; not heeded; not regarded; unmarked. ''Byron'', Corsair, i.—'''2.''' Not marked or shown outwardly. ''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 5. 21. [Rare.] '''unnoticed''' (un-nō′tisd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not observed; not regarded; not noted; unmarked. {{smaller block|How superior in dignity, as well as in number, are the ''unnoticed'', unhonored saints and heroes of domestic and humble life. {{right|''Channing'', in Kidd’s Rhetorical Reader, p. 217.}}}} '''2.''' Not treated with the usual marks of re-
readings.c3s3:
spect; not entertained with due attentions; neglected.

'''unnotify''' (un-nō′ti-fī), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''notify.''] To negative, as something previously made known, declared, or notified. ''H. Walpole'', To Mann, iii. 231. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''unnumberable''' (un-num′bėr-a-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unnombirable; < un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''numberable.''] Innumerable.

'''unnumbered''' (un-num′bėrd), ''a.'' Not numbered; hence, innumerable; indefinitely numerous. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iv.

'''unnumerable†''' (un-nū′me̤-ra̤-bl), ''a.'' Innumerable. [Rare.]

'''unnun''' (un-nun′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''nun.''] To release or depose from the condition of a nun; cause to cease to be a nun. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Many did quickly ''unnun'' and disfriar themselves.
{{right|''Fuller.''}}}}

'''unnurtured''' (un-nėr′tṳ̄rd), ''a.'' Not nurtured; not educated; untrained; rough.
{{smaller block|<poem>“''Unnurtured'' Blount!—thy brawling cease;
He opes his eyes,” said Eustace; “peace!”</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, vi. 28.}}}}

'''unobedience†''' (un-ọ̄-bē′di-e̤ns), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unobedience; < un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''obedience.''] Disobedience. ''Wyclif'', 2 Cor. x.

'''unobedient†''' (un-ọ̄-bē′di-e̤nt), ''a.'' Disobedient.
{{smaller block|Pepin, not ''unobedient'' to the Popes call, passing into Italy, frees him out of danger.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}
